entries.clue: Not a complete arse  though decapitated farm animals (7)

indicatorNotes.decapitated: Decapitating a thing takes its head off, and the head of a word is the letter it begins with.

blocks.note: but is the little word that does the work of though
the animals kept on a farm are stock, and the head letter is cut away

annotation.surface: A man judged not a complete idiot, beside some farm animals that have lost their heads.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Arse' does double duty: the insult the surface throws, and the anatomy the definition means one half of. Stock for the animals on a farm is the word hiding inside livestock.
annotation.definitionFit: An arse is two cheeks, so one of them falls short of a complete one — the definition names the part by what it is missing.

entries.clue: In the sack, drunk starts to take exercise  potty! (8)

indicatorNotes.In: In names the place, so the word just after it is the one everything else is put inside.
indicatorNotes.starts: The start of a word is its opening letter, so only the first letter of each word named is taken.

blocks.note: the sack is slang for bed, as in hitting the sack
a sot is a habitual drunk
the opening letters of take and exercise, in that order

annotation.surface: A drunk in bed beginning his workout, which is plainly mad.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Potty' is British for mad, and the sense wanted is the narrow one — potty about a person rather than potty in general. SOT for a drunk is old and faintly literary.
annotation.definitionFit: Besotted means so taken with someone that judgement has gone, which is what calling a lover potty about them says.

entries.clue: Chuck's worth getting stuffed (5)

indicatorNotes.getting stuffed: Stuffing a thing crams its contents in at any angle, so the letters end up in a different order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters

annotation.surface: A man called Chuck deserves to be stuffed, like a trophy on a wall.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Chuck' is placed to look like a name and is a verb. The indicator is the rude sense of stuffed, which does exactly the job any politer word for cramming would do.
annotation.definitionFit: To chuck something is to throw it — the everyday British verb for lobbing a thing away.

entries.clue: Colleague needs right air to be suitable (9)

blocks.note: oppo is British slang for a workmate, short for opposite number
r is the standard short form for right
an air is a melody

annotation.surface: A colleague needs the right atmosphere before he will do.
annotation.walkthrough: An air is a tune in the old musical sense, the word behind 'Air on a G String'; the surface reads it as atmosphere instead. Oppo for a colleague is forces and police slang.
annotation.definitionFit: What is opportune suits the moment exactly, so a well-timed offer is a suitable one.

entries.clue: As Keir represented Bill? (6)

indicatorNotes.represented: To re-present something is to present it afresh in another arrangement, which is what these letters get.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters

annotation.surface: Keir Starmer standing in for a man called Bill.
annotation.walkthrough: Wilhelm II, Germany's emperor through the First World War, was Bill to the British press, and his title is what the clue is after. Keir is Sir Keir Starmer, Labour's prime minister.
annotation.definitionFit: Britain nicknamed Wilhelm II 'Bill', so the name on its own stands for the German emperor's title, kaiser.

entries.clue: Friday commandeered by mad Crusoe to adjust telescope? (7)

indicatorNotes.commandeered by: Something commandeered has been seized and carried off by whoever took it, so this letter joins the letters that follow.
indicatorNotes.mad: A mad thing has lost its proper order, and letters out of their proper order have to be rearranged.

blocks.note: f is the day's short form on a timetable
anagram fodder, six letters, with the day's letter joined in

annotation.surface: A deranged Robinson Crusoe seizes Man Friday and fiddles with his telescope.
annotation.walkthrough: Friday is Crusoe's companion in Defoe's novel and here supplies nothing but the weekday's initial. The question mark concedes that a telescope is only one of the things you might do this to.
annotation.definitionFit: To refocus is to reset a lens until the image comes back sharp, which is the adjustment a telescope keeps needing.

entries.clue: Wifeless like Lee Anderson and making amends (8)

indicatorNotes.Wifeless: Less on the end of a word means without, so the letter that stands for a wife is taken out of the description that follows.

blocks.note: Lee Anderson is chairman of Reform UK and sits on the hard right of British politics
w is the standard short form for wife, and it is the letter dropped

annotation.surface: Lee Anderson, with no wife, is busy putting things right.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole of the wordplay is one hyphenated description of the man, a letter lighter. Anderson chairs Reform UK, Nigel Farage's party, and is a byword in Britain for the hard right.
annotation.definitionFit: Righting a wrong is setting it straight again, which is what making amends amounts to.

entries.clue: Gross Washington religious order (5)

blocks.note: a gross figure is a fat one
WA is the US postal code for Washington state

annotation.surface: A disgusting religious decree comes out of Washington.
annotation.walkthrough: Washington here is the state rather than the capital or the president, and its two-letter postal code is all the clue takes. 'Gross' wants the plain adjective for fat, not the surface's revulsion.
annotation.definitionFit: A fatwa is a ruling handed down by an Islamic authority, so it is an order issued on religious grounds.

entries.clue: Mistress sure to rot in jail (9)

indicatorNotes.rot: Rotting matter falls apart and its pieces settle in a new arrangement, which is what happens to these letters.
indicatorNotes.in: 'in' names where a thing goes, so the letters before it are set inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: the can is slang for prison
the six letters of sure to in another order

annotation.surface: A mistress is certain to rot away in prison.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rot' is the shuffling instruction and the surface's prison fate at once, which is why the sentence runs so smoothly. The can for prison is American slang long since naturalised in Britain.
annotation.definitionFit: A courtesan is a kept mistress, historically one attached to a court or a wealthy household.

entries.clue: Gorgeous detective casually mounts bishop (6)

indicatorNotes.mounts: In a down clue whatever mounts climbs on top, so the letters before it are written above the letter that follows.

blocks.note: a police superintendent is the super in casual speech
b is the bishop on a chess scoresheet

annotation.surface: An off-duty detective climbing on top of a bishop.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Casually' is not padding: it licenses the clipped form of superintendent that officers actually use. The mounting is vertical, which is the only direction a down entry offers.
annotation.definitionFit: Superb means of the finest quality, which is the claim calling a thing gorgeous makes.

entries.clue: Strong and into S and M? (9)

annotation.definitionNote: The second half describes a person's taste rather than defining a word: what someone into S and M is into is the noun, the use of straps, while the first half is the adjective for big and well-built.

blocks.note: the sense used of a big, well-built lad rather than of a taste or a drink
sadomasochism runs on whips, chains and straps, and the noun names the use of them

annotation.surface: A big strong type who is also keen on whips and chains.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are definitions, which is why nothing in the clue asks for a letter to be moved. S and M is sadomasochism, and the second half teases rather than defines — Cyclops's usual register.
annotation.definitionFit: A strapping lad is powerfully built, and strapping is also the business of straps that sadomasochism turns on.

entries.clue: (& 11ac.) Old fart, one who pulls president's erection (5)

blocks.note: to trump is an old word for breaking wind
whoever tows a thing is a tow-er, the agent noun said with a long o

annotation.surface: An old fart turns out to be the one tugging at the president's erection.
annotation.walkthrough: The second piece is the agent noun from 'tow' — one who tows — said with a long o. The definition carries the joke: an erection is anything put up, and this president put his name on it.
annotation.definitionFit: Trump Tower is the Manhattan skyscraper Donald Trump built and named after himself, so the president's erection is literally his own building.

entries.clue: see 10ac. (5)
Fan, say, of T.Rex screwed by player (9)

indicatorNotes.screwed: Something screwed has been twisted out of true, and letters twisted out of true come back in another order.

blocks.note: the four letters of T REX in another order
a player is an actor, the old theatre word for one

annotation.surface: A fan of T.Rex gets cheated by one of the band.
annotation.walkthrough: T.Rex was Marc Bolan's glam-rock band, so 'player' reads as a musician and means an actor. 'Fan, say' is a definition by example: the kind that shifts air, not the kind that buys records.
annotation.definitionFit: An extractor is the fan that pulls stale air out of a kitchen or a bathroom, so it is one sort of fan — which 'say' concedes.

entries.clue: Topless, weepy, getting a bollocking (6)

indicatorNotes.Topless: Something topless has lost its top, and the top of a word is the letter it begins with.

blocks.note: someone weepy is tearful, and the top letter then goes

annotation.surface: A topless woman in tears is being told off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Topless' plays both its senses at once: the Private Eye picture and the instruction to drop a first letter. A bollocking is British slang for a fierce dressing-down.
annotation.definitionFit: An earful is a torrent of abuse poured into somebody's ear, which is what a bollocking delivers.

entries.clue: Balance requires EU supporter to accept date (9)

indicatorNotes.to accept: To accept a thing is to take it in, so the letter named after it goes inside the word before.

blocks.note: in the Brexit argument those who wanted Britain to stay in the EU were Remainers
d is the standard short form for date

annotation.surface: A pro-EU campaigner has to agree to a date.
annotation.walkthrough: Remainer was the label for the anti-Brexit side in the 2016 referendum, and it has to be read as one word rather than a phrase. 'Balance' wants the accountant's sense: what is left.
annotation.definitionFit: The remainder is what is left once the rest has been taken away, which is the balance of a sum or an account.

entries.clue: Powerful trendy present, maybe (7)

blocks.note: what is in is what is fashionable
the present is one of the tenses, which is what maybe concedes

annotation.surface: A gift that happens to be fashionable.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Present' is the grammarian's tense here rather than the parcel, and 'maybe' is in the clue because the present is only one tense among several.
annotation.definitionFit: An intense heat or an intense effort is a concentrated one, which is what calling it powerful says.

entries.clue: (& 27ac.) Overexcited, rue going bananas for Trump-style legislation (9)

indicatorNotes.going bananas: To go bananas is to go completely wild, and letters gone wild have to be put back in a different order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, fourteen letters

annotation.surface: Regret goes berserk in the excitement over the president's way of making law.
annotation.walkthrough: An executive order is a presidential decree that bypasses Congress, so 'Trump-style legislation' is a jab as well as a definition. 'Rue' is the noun — regret — which is what keeps the surface upright.
annotation.definitionFit: Trump governs by executive order, signing decrees that do the work of law without Congress ever voting.

entries.clue: Labour dupe agitated and upset (6,2)

indicatorNotes.agitated: Agitating something shakes its contents about, so these letters are shaken into a new order.

blocks.note: labour and work are the same toil
the four letters of dupe in another order

annotation.surface: A gullible Labour voter is stirred up and left distressed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Labour' is capitalised for the party and wanted for plain toil. The four shuffled letters straddle the gap between the answer's two words, so the enumeration is no help in placing them.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone worked up is agitated and smarting, which is what upset says of a person's state.

entries.clue: Bully, whiskey-covered Republican, put away (8)

indicatorNotes.covered: In a down clue what covers a thing lies over the top of it, so these letters are written above the letter that follows.

blocks.note: a single malt is whiskey
R is the party's letter beside a candidate's name on a US ballot
to put food away is to eat it

annotation.surface: A Republican drenched in whiskey is bullied and then locked up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Put away' is imprisonment in the surface and eating in the wordplay. The covering is vertical: in a down entry the whiskey lies over the party letter rather than wrapping round it.
annotation.definitionFit: To maltreat someone is to handle them cruelly, which is what a bully does to a victim.

entries.clue: English politician at fault dropping Reform's first leader (7)

indicatorNotes.dropping: Dropping a letter takes it out of what has been assembled so far.
indicatorNotes.first: The first of a name is the letter it starts with, and that is the letter named here.

blocks.note: e is the standard short form for English
an MP is a Member of Parliament
someone at fault is in error, with one letter then taken out
the opening letter of Reform UK, Nigel Farage's party, and the letter dropped

annotation.surface: An English MP in the wrong after Reform's first leader is dropped.
annotation.walkthrough: Reform UK is Nigel Farage's party and the clue takes only the R it starts with. 'Leader' is the definition, sitting at the end of a sentence about party leadership so that it reads as part of the story.
annotation.definitionFit: An emperor is the man at the head of an empire, so he is a leader in the plainest sense of the word.

entries.clue: Protrusion of organ: the woman's in a whirl (6)

indicatorNotes.whirl: A whirl spins whatever is caught up in it, so these letters come to rest in a different order.

blocks.note: what belongs to the woman is hers, and her is that possessive
the three letters of in a in another order

annotation.surface: A woman is in a spin about somebody's organ.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder is two words a solver reads straight past — 'in a' — and the colon does nothing beyond staging the surface. 'The woman's' wants the possessive pronoun, not a name.
annotation.definitionFit: A hernia is an organ pushing out through the wall that should contain it, which is exactly a protrusion of organ.

entries.clue: Bling, perhaps, offered by streetwise guy round church (6)

blocks.note: bro is street slang for a mate
the letter drawn as a circle
ch is how church is abbreviated on a map

annotation.surface: A street-smart lad hands over some jewellery outside a church.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like the preposition that would wrap one piece about another and is simply the letter shaped like a circle. Bling is 1990s hip-hop slang for showy jewellery, which 'perhaps' narrows to one item.
annotation.definitionFit: A brooch is a jewelled pin worn to be noticed, so it counts as bling — 'perhaps' conceding it is only one kind.

entries.clue: Rock's at London university, failing that (2,4)

blocks.note: ore is the rock a metal is dug out of
the London School of Economics, on Houghton Street off the Strand

annotation.surface: Rock music has made it onto the syllabus at a London university.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rock' is the geologist's here, not the guitarist's. LSE is the London School of Economics, whose initials are the standard shorthand for a London university.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Or else' is how an ultimatum ends — do this, failing that, and here is what follows.

entries.clue: One claiming to cause downfall of Iran  fantastic supreme being! (9)

indicatorNotes.fantastic: Something fantastic is wildly out of the ordinary, and letters out of their ordinary order have to be rearranged.

blocks.note: the four letters of Iran in another order
the Maker is God, as in 'meet your Maker'

annotation.surface: A man boasts that he can bring Iran down, and salutes a fantastic god.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Downfall' is a regime's collapse in the surface and the falling of rain in the definition. The exclamation mark belongs to the surface's enthusiasm and carries no instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A rainmaker claims to bring the rain down, by ritual or by seeding clouds, so the downfall promised is the weather's.

entries.clue: Often seen before Christmas, pissed (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The first half does not define the word at all but says where it is usually printed — immediately in front of Christmas — which is fair play as long as the other half is a true synonym.

blocks.note: the word that heads the greeting on every card in the shop
British slang for drunk, and the other half of the clue wants the politer word for that state

annotation.surface: Drunk in the weeks running up to Christmas.
annotation.walkthrough: One half is a synonym and the other is a position: the word wanted is the one that habitually stands in front of 'Christmas'. 'Pissed' is British for drunk, not the American sense of annoyed.
annotation.definitionFit: Merry is the word that always precedes Christmas in the greeting, and merry is also long-standing British slang for tipsy.

entries.clue: Finished sexual initiation with alien  pissed off (5)

indicatorNotes.initiation: An initiation is a beginning, so only the opening letter of the word in front of it is taken.

blocks.note: when time is up it is finished
the opening letter of sexual
ET is the film's extra-terrestrial and the crossword's standard alien

annotation.surface: A first sexual experience with an extraterrestrial, now over, has left somebody annoyed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Initiation' reads as a first sexual experience and asks for a first letter. 'Finished' wants the up of 'time's up', which is how two letters come out of one short word.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone upset has been put out and is smarting about it, which is what pissed off says more bluntly.

entries.clue: Poles, in picture, smell? (5)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' names the place a thing goes, so the letters before it are set inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: to picture a thing is to see it in the mind
N and S are the two poles of a magnet or a compass

annotation.surface: Some Poles turn up in a photograph and apparently smell.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital P offers Polish people and the clue means the magnetic pair. 'Smell?' is a definition by example — one of the five — with the question mark admitting as much.
annotation.definitionFit: Smell is one of the five senses, so the clue names the class by a single member of it.

entries.clue: see 16dn.
Trifling Democrat coalition (9)

blocks.note: D is the party's letter beside a candidate's name on a US ballot
an alliance is a coalition of parties or powers

annotation.surface: A Democrat's unimportant coalition deal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trifling' is the noun — the act of trifling — and not the adjective meaning trivial that the surface offers. A dalliance can be a flirtation or merely a half-hearted go at something.
annotation.definitionFit: A dalliance is dabbling or flirting, so trifling, the act of not taking a thing seriously, names it.

entries.clue: Press on about Murphy losing head without Rugby Union backing (5,2)

indicatorNotes.about: Letters said to be about are out of their places rather than in them, so they have to be set down in a fresh order.
indicatorNotes.losing head: A head is the letter at the front, and losing it drops that letter from the name.
indicatorNotes.without: Without is used in its older sense of outside, so the letters already assembled close around the pair that follows.
indicatorNotes.backing: Backing a thing turns it to face the other way, so its two letters are written in reverse.

blocks.note: Murphy gives up its head letter and the five that remain are re-ordered
rugby union is RU, turned round to face the other way

annotation.surface: The papers keep going on about Murphy losing his head now that Rugby Union will not back him.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Without' is doing the old job of outside rather than the modern one of lacking, which is what puts the turned pair inside the shuffle. 'Press on' is the definition, though the surface offers newspapers.
annotation.definitionFit: To hurry up is to get a move on, and press on is the same instruction — keep going, and faster.

entries.clue: Keele men try storing carbon? (7)

indicatorNotes.storing: Something storing another thing keeps it whole inside itself, so the letters sit unbroken in the words before.

blocks.note: the seven letters run on without a break across the three words

annotation.surface: Men at Keele University are trying to store carbon.
annotation.walkthrough: Keele is a university in Staffordshire, and the run begins inside its name — three ordinary words with a seam in the middle of the first. 'Carbon?' names one member of the class, which the question mark flags.
annotation.definitionFit: Carbon is one of the chemical elements, so the clue points at the class by naming a single example of it.
